steps.body: A shape has a **line of symmetry** if folding along that line makes both halves land exactly on top of each other — like a mirror. A square folded straight down the middle matches perfectly. A random scribbled shape usually doesn't.
Test a fold by comparing the two halves it creates.

widget.prompt: A fold line makes the left and right halves land exactly on each other. What is true of this fold?
widget.witness: Folding the shape makes every point on one half meet its partner on the other half.

choices.label: Always a symmetry line
choices.feedback: A perfect-match fold is exactly the definition of a line of symmetry.

choices.label: Sometimes a symmetry line
choices.feedback: If the halves match exactly, the fold qualifies every time.
choices.evidenceText: There is no unmatched part in the stated fold.

choices.label: Never a symmetry line
choices.feedback: This reverses the definition: exact matching is the evidence for symmetry.

widget.fallbackFeedback: A line of symmetry is a fold line that makes the two halves match exactly.
widget.successFeedback: The fold is a line of symmetry because the two halves coincide exactly.

predict.prompt: A fold line counts as a line of SYMMETRY when the two halves…?
predict.reveal: Symmetry demands a perfect overlap — every point landing on its twin. Equal areas or a family resemblance isn't enough; the fold must make the halves disappear into each other.

explanationVariants: If folding along a line makes both halves match exactly, that line is a line of symmetry.
A perfect match after folding is the whole test.

widget.prompt: Folding a shape along a certain line makes the two halves match perfectly, like a mirror. What is this line called?

options.label: A line of symmetry
options.feedback: A fold line that produces a perfect match is a line of symmetry.

options.label: A perpendicular line
options.feedback: Perpendicular describes two lines crossing at 90° — a different idea entirely. A perfect-match fold line is a line of symmetry.

options.label: A diagonal
options.feedback: A diagonal is just a line connecting two corners — it isn't automatically a symmetry line unless folding along it produces a match.

options.label: A ray
options.feedback: A ray has one endpoint and extends forever one way. A fold line that matches both halves is a line of symmetry.

steps.body: Not every line through a shape works. A square has SOME lines that produce a match (straight down the middle, or corner to corner) and infinitely many that don't (any random slanted line off-center). Only the special ones count as symmetry lines.

explanationVariants: A fold line placed off-center won't produce matching halves, even in an otherwise symmetric shape.
Position matters — not just any line through the shape counts.

widget.prompt: A square is folded along a line that's close to the middle, but not exactly centered. Do the halves match?

options.label: No — an off-center fold doesn't produce a true match
options.feedback: Only the exact center lines (or exact diagonals) of a square produce matching halves. Close isn't enough.

options.label: Yes — it's a square, so any fold works
options.feedback: Being a square doesn't mean EVERY fold works — only the specific center and diagonal lines produce true matches.

options.label: Yes, since it's close to the middle
options.feedback: Close to center still isn't exact — the two halves would be slightly different sizes, so they wouldn't truly match.

options.label: It depends on the square's size
options.feedback: Size doesn't matter — the fold's exact POSITION does. An off-center line fails no matter how big the square is.

widget.prompt: Sort each fold: do the halves match, or not?

items.label: A circle, folded through its exact center, any direction
items.feedback: Every fold through a circle's center produces a perfect match.

items.label: An arrow shape (pointing one way), folded top to bottom
items.feedback: The pointed end and flat end don't match — no fold lines them up this way.

items.label: A regular hexagon, folded through two opposite corners
items.feedback: Regular hexagons have several matching fold lines, including corner to corner.

items.label: The letter F, folded down the middle
items.feedback: F's top and bottom halves are different shapes — no fold produces a match.

widget.missFeedback: Picture the actual fold and check whether every point lines up with a matching point.
widget.successFeedback: Circles and regular hexagons fold into matches; an arrow and the letter F don't.

explanationVariants: A shape with no matching sides or angles anywhere has no fold that produces matching halves.
Some shapes genuinely have zero lines of symmetry.

widget.prompt: A shape has three sides, all different lengths, and three different angles. How many lines of symmetry does it have?

options.label: 0 — no fold produces matching halves
options.feedback: With no matching sides or angles anywhere, no single fold line can make the two halves match.

options.label: 1 — every shape has at least one
options.feedback: Not every shape has a symmetry line. With all sides and angles different, there's genuinely none here.

options.label: 3 — one per side
options.feedback: That pattern only holds for shapes with EQUAL sides. With all different sides, there are 0 symmetry lines.

options.label: It's impossible to have zero
options.feedback: It's entirely possible — an irregular shape with no matching parts anywhere has 0 lines of symmetry.

hints: A stop sign is a regular octagon — all 8 sides and angles equal.
Picture folding it through the center in different directions.
A shape with all equal sides folds into matching halves in multiple ways.
explanationVariants: A regular octagon's equal sides and angles mean many different fold lines through the center all produce matching halves.
Equal sides everywhere means the fold test succeeds repeatedly.

widget.prompt: A stop sign is shaped like a regular octagon — 8 equal sides and 8 equal angles. Folding it straight down the middle through two opposite corners: do the halves match?

options.label: Yes — equal sides and angles mean this fold produces a match
options.feedback: With every side and angle equal, folding through opposite corners lines up matching pieces on both sides.

options.label: No — octagons are too complex to fold evenly
options.feedback: Having many sides doesn't prevent symmetry — the sides being EQUAL is what allows this fold to succeed.

options.label: Only if the octagon is very large
options.feedback: Size doesn't affect whether a fold produces a match — the equal sides and angles do, regardless of scale.

options.label: Can't tell without trying every possible fold
options.feedback: The equal-sides-and-angles rule already tells us this particular fold, through opposite corners, succeeds.

takeaways: A line of symmetry is a fold line where both halves land on top of each other exactly.
Not every line through a shape works — only specific, well-placed ones.
Shapes with no matching sides or angles can have zero lines of symmetry.
steps.teaser: next: counting exactly how many symmetry lines different shapes have.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **A line of symmetry makes both halves match when folded.** Picture a butterfly: fold it down the middle of its body, and both wings line up perfectly — that fold line is a line of symmetry.

explanationVariants: Folding down the middle of a butterfly's body matches both wings perfectly.
A perfect match after folding is the definition.

widget.prompt: Folding a butterfly picture down the middle of its body makes both wings match exactly. Is this a line of symmetry?

options.label: Yes
options.feedback: A perfect match after folding is exactly what a line of symmetry means.

options.label: No, wings are never identical
options.feedback: In a simple symmetric drawing, the wings DO match — that's what makes this fold a line of symmetry.

options.label: Only real butterflies count
options.feedback: The test is whether the fold produces a match, in a drawing or in real life — either way, matching wings mean symmetry.
